findings: R2's ORIGINAL FINDING, NOW CONFIRMED LANDED IN game/src/sim/camera.js AT HEAD (no diff in the working tree -- this is not my edit, I am verifying a predecessor's swept-in work): the up vector in basis() was built as up = right x fwd, which at yaw=0/pitch=0 is (0,-1,0) -- pointing at the ground -- and up.y = -cos(pitch) for the WHOLE legal pitch band. project()'s NDC y was therefore sign-inverted, and containSteer's `(tY>0?1:-1)*rate` correction drove the pitch AWAY from the target: a positive-feedback loop that ran to the -50 deg locked floor and pinned the view down for the rest of any fight, PAST the kill. The current source (game/src/sim/camera.js:552-643, function lockOrientation) now measures the pitch target's elevation over the PIVOT (pitch-independent baseline) instead of the camera's own pitch-dependent position, which was the actual closed loop (comment block at line 573 attributes it precisely: loop gain G ~= +2.5 at the mid-boss case, and a gain above 1 does not settle, it runs to whichever clamp the initial sign points at).

CONFIRMED WITH tools/camera/cam-pitch-instrument.mjs (already built, committed, not part-built as the dispatch text guessed) run fresh this round: --table settles mid-boss at pitch +9.377 deg (not the -50 floor); --gain reports loop_gain_G ~ 0 (a contraction) with 0.000 spread across six different starting pitches for every (h,d) row, i.e. the answer no longer depends on where the lock happened to start; --m2 (RI-CAM03 SE M2, the item's own falsifier) passes 5/5 with residual error <=0.17 deg against the declared pitch_bias(d,h); --contain confirms the NDC sign now agrees with a ground-truth, independently-built view basis (sim_ndc_sign_agrees_with_truth: true). All four exit 0.

RULES.md rule 4/6 applied: this is the falsifier written IN the tool by the r2 agent (attractors()/m2Residual()) rather than something I had to invent -- reverting the pitch reference (measuring elevation from c.pos instead of c.pivot) is the documented one-line regression that makes --gain go back above 1 on its own; I did not need to hand-break it because the tool already carries its own delete-the-fix.
